content: A pterygium is a benign, whitish-pink, triangular-shaped growth of tissue on the conjunctiva, the clear membrane covering the white part of the eye. It most commonly originates from the nasal side of the eye and extends toward the cornea. While it rarely grows large enough to cover the pupil, its growth patterns can vary; some pterygia grow slowly over a lifetime, while others stop growing at a certain point. It can affect one or both eyes. The hallmark symptom of a pterygium is a painless, elevated area of whitish-pink tissue with visible blood vessels, typically located on the inner or outer edge of the cornea. The exact cause of pterygium development remains unknown. This has led many experts to believe that UV radiation from the sun plays a key role in its formation. Pterygium is most frequently observed in individuals aged 20 to 40 who live in sunny, dry climates. Chronic dry eye is also thought to contribute to its development. Occupations such as farming and fishing, as well as living near the equator, are associated with a higher prevalence of pterygium. Pterygium is rarely seen in children. Diagnosis of a pterygium is typically made through a physical examination of the eyes and eyelids. Special diagnostic tests are generally unnecessary. Urgent medical care is not usually required for pterygium. However, if the growth begins to impair vision, it is important to consult an ophthalmologist for treatment. Annual eye examinations are recommended for individuals with pterygium to monitor the condition and address any potential vision issues early. Patients who have had a pterygium in the past should also see an eye doctor if symptoms recur. Treatment is not necessary unless the pterygium begins to obstruct vision. Lubricating eye drops can help alleviate redness and irritation. If the pterygium affects vision, surgical removal is recommended. Some individuals may seek surgical removal for cosmetic reasons, but this is generally not advised unless vision is compromised. Recurrence of the pterygium after surgery is common, particularly in patients under 40 years of age. In cases of recurrence or when the regrowth threatens vision, strontium-90 (90Sr) plaque therapy may be used. This treatment involves the application of a radioactive substance that emits beta particles, which penetrate a short distance into the cornea to suppress the regrowth of blood vessels. The procedure is typically performed under local anesthesia and is best done at the time of, or shortly after, pterygium excision. Conditions with similar symptoms include pinguecula, which should be considered in the differential diagnosis. To prevent pterygium, individuals in areas with strong sunlight are advised to wear protective eyewear, such as sunglasses or eyeglasses, and hats with wide brims. Most pterygia do not cause significant problems and do not require treatment. If a pterygium affects vision or the cornea, surgical removal generally yields good outcomes. However, recurrence is possible after removal.
